subject: How to handle uninterested missing (unobserved) data?

messages.author: 40b63348dbcb447d
messages.subject: How to handle uninterested missing (unobserved) data?
parts:
Hi all,

Suppose I have N items {x_n}_{n=1}^N (and also denote the feature vector as x_n) and I have observed M pairwise preferences {x_{i_m} \succ x_{j_m}}_{m=1}^M from a user. Now I want to predict this user's preference on an unseen pair x_i and x_j. I first assume a utility function f, such that f(x_i) > f(x_j) <=> x_i \succ x_j <=> y_{ij} = 1. Then I suppose the probability of the preference is given by

Pr(y_{ij}=1) = 1/(1+exp[f(x_j)-f(x_i)])

also let f be a Gaussian process:

f ~ GP(0, Σ)

In this way I'll have a generative model. But of course I don't have all the preferences in the training data. If I define Y=(y_{ij}) as an n-by-n matrix in data block, it seems I need to give all the entries in Y. I don't want to put it into the parameters block because I am not interested in all the pairs. What is the correct way to handle this in stan? Thank you.

Best,
Ziyuan

messages.author: 743bbacc59f4b25f
messages.subject: Re: How to handle uninterested missing (unobserved) data?
parts:
You can use increment_log_prob() as many times as you need to, but there is no shortcut in Stan. Stan doesn't have a missing value code or a convenient way to have known data and unknown parameters in the same container.

Basically, you need to pass Y in as data perhaps with -999 as the code for missing cells. Then, you need to declare a vector of parameters like Y_miss whose length is equal to the number of missing cells in Y. Then in the the model block do

model {
  matrix[n,n] Y_complete;
  int count;
  count <- 1
  for(i in 1:n) for(j in 1:n) {
    if(Y[i,j] == -999) {
      Y_complete[i,j] <- Y_miss[count];
      count <- count + 1;
    }
    else Y_complete[i,j] <- Y[i,j];
  }
}

Finally, evaluate the likelihood of Y_complete and your priors. Y_miss will get stored but you can just ignore it for the most part.

Ben

messages.author: 743bbacc59f4b25f
messages.subject: Re: How to handle uninterested missing (unobserved) data?
parts:
Yes, Y_miss is part of the posterior (presuming you do not have a clever way to integrate it out) and Stan samples from the joint posterior. As to whether it is inefficient, it depends on what you mean by that. The Stan code is longer and uglier. It takes a lot more time, and RAM, and disk space (if you write to a file) to sample and if you do not care about Y_miss, then the only benefit to it is that it ensures you have a valid basis for interference on the margins of the posterior that you do care about (which are generally not independent of Y_miss). But otherwise, you have a valid basis for interference only under strong assumptions about the missingness mechanism(s).

The stan() function in rstan has a pars argument that you can use to exclude Y_miss from the reported results but it still is part of the model. I hope that in 2015, Stan will be better in situations like this, both by handing missing values in a cleaner way and having the capability to integrate out nuisance parameters.

Ben

messages.author: 743bbacc59f4b25f
messages.subject: Re: How to handle uninterested missing (unobserved) data?
parts:
As to whether that is valid Stan code, yes, you could do something like

for(i in 1:n) for(j in 1:n) if(Y[i,j] != -999) increment_log_prob(...);

but you don't even have to use increment_log_prob(), you could use

Y[i,j] ~ normal(X[idx[i]] * beta + X[idx[j]] * gamma, sigma);

or something. But you would be using the observed data likelihood, rather than the complete data likelihood, and also ignoring the contribution to the likelihood of to_vector(Y == -999) given the complete data.

Ben
